1: # AGENTS.md
2: 
3: This document describes how to develop and document the `mlt` codebase for AI coding agents and human contributors.
4: 
5: ## Project Overview
6: 
7: `mlt` (pronounced "melt") is an ultra-fast, extensible linter for MATLAB written in Rust. It uses `tree-sitter-matlab` for parsing and is architecturally inspired by [ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) and [rumdl](https://github.com/rvben/rumdl).
8: 
9: The goal is full feature parity with MATLAB's Code Analyzer (~2,680 checks), using the same check IDs (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `naming.class.casing`).
10: 
11: ## Workspace Structure
12: 
13: ```
14: mlt/
15: ├── Cargo.toml              # Workspace root (resolver = "2")
16: ├── zensical.toml           # Documentation site config (Zensical/MkDocs)
17: ├── crates/
18: │   ├── mlt_cli/            # CLI binary (clap, config discovery, output formatting)
19: │   ├── mlt_core/           # Core engine (Rule trait, RuleRegistry, Linter, Config, Diagnostic)
20: │   └── mlt_rules/          # Individual lint rule implementations
21: └── docs/                   # Zensical documentation site (Markdown)
22: ```
23: 
24: ### Crate Responsibilities
25: 
26: | Crate | Purpose |
27: |-------|---------|
28: | `mlt_core` | Defines `Rule` trait, `Category` enum, `NodeContext`/`FileContext`, `RuleRegistry`, `Linter` engine, `Config` parsing, `Diagnostic`/`Fix`/`Severity` types. No concrete rules live here. |
29: | `mlt_rules` | All concrete rule implementations. Uses `inventory` crate for auto-registration. Exports `all_rules(&Config)` and `active_rules(&Config)`. Depends on `mlt_core`. |
30: | `mlt_cli` | Binary entry point. Discovers `.mlt.toml`, builds registry, invokes linter, formats output. Depends on both `mlt_core` and `mlt_rules`. |
31: 
32: ### Dependency Direction
33: 
34: ```
35: mlt_cli → mlt_rules → mlt_core
36: ```
37: 
38: `mlt_core` has zero internal dependencies. `mlt_rules` depends only on `mlt_core`. `mlt_cli` depends on both.
39: 
40: ## Architecture
41: 
42: ### Lint Engine Flow
43: 
44: 1. CLI loads `.mlt.toml` → parses into `Config`
45: 2. `mlt_rules::active_rules(&config)` → constructs only enabled rules (filtered by per-rule and per-category config)
46: 3. `RuleRegistry::new(rules, &config)` → indexes rules by `target_node_types()`, resolves effective severity per rule (per-rule > per-category > rule default)
47: 4. `Linter::new(registry)` → initializes tree-sitter parser with MATLAB grammar
48: 5. `linter.lint(source, file_path)` → single-pass DFS traversal:
49:    - For each node: O(1) lookup of subscribed rules, dispatch `rule.check(&NodeContext)`
50:    - After traversal: call `rule.check_file(&FileContext)` only on rules where `has_file_check() == true`
51:    - Stamp effective severity (config override) onto all diagnostics
52:    - Return sorted diagnostics
53: 
54: ### Rule Trait
55: 
56: ```rust
57: pub trait Rule: Send + Sync {
58:     fn id(&self) -> &'static str;                          // e.g., "NOSEMI"
59:     fn description(&self) -> &'static str;                 // One-line summary
60:     fn severity(&self) -> Severity;                        // Default severity
61:     fn category(&self) -> Category;                        // Rule category for bulk config
62:     fn target_node_types(&self) -> &'static [&'static str]; // Node types to subscribe to
63: 
64:     fn can_be_disabled(&self) -> bool { true }             // false for critical checks
65:     fn has_file_check(&self) -> bool { false }             // true if check_file is implemented
66: 
67:     fn check(&self, ctx: &NodeContext) -> Vec<Diagnostic> { vec![] }      // Per-node
68:     fn check_file(&self, ctx: &FileContext) -> Vec<Diagnostic> { vec![] } // Per-file
69: }
70: ```
71: 
72: - **Node-level rules**: Implement `check()`, return non-empty `target_node_types()`.
73: - **File-level rules**: Implement `check_file()`, set `has_file_check() → true`, return empty `target_node_types()`.
74: - **Hybrid**: Implement both (rare).
75: 
76: ### Rule Categories
77: 
78: Rules are organized into categories matching MATLAB's Code Analyzer groups:
79: 
80: | Category Enum | Config Key | Description |
81: |---------------|-----------|-------------|
82: | `IncompleteAnalysis` | `incomplete-analysis` | Internal linter limits |
83: | `SyntaxErrors` | `syntax-errors` | Parser-level validation |
84: | `LanguageSpecification` | `language-specification` | Language constraint violations |
85: | `Bugs` | `bugs` | Likely bugs and logic errors |
86: | `CustomChecks` | `custom-checks` | Complexity/style metrics |
87: | `Naming` | `naming` | Naming conventions |
88: | `Compatibility` | `compatibility` | Deprecated/removed APIs |
89: | `ForwardCompatibility` | `forward-compatibility` | Forward compatibility |
90: | `GoodPractices` | `good-practices` | Best practices |
91: | `UnsetVariables` | `unset-variables` | Undefined variables |
92: | `UnusedConstructions` | `unused-constructions` | Dead code |
93: | `SuggestedImprovements` | `suggested-improvements` | Code improvement suggestions |
94: | `Readability` | `readability` | Readability improvements |
95: | `Formatting` | `formatting` | Code formatting |
96: | `Performance` | `performance` | Performance hints |
97: | `CodeGeneration` | `code-generation` | MATLAB Coder constraints |
98: | `FixedPoint` | `fixed-point` | Fixed-point toolbox |
99: | `Deployment` | `deployment` | MATLAB Compiler constraints |
100: | `SystemObjects` | `system-objects` | System object validation |
101: | `Unsupported` | `unsupported` | Unsupported features |
102: | `BehaviorChanges` | `behavior-changes` | Version behavior changes |
103: | `ConfigurationIssues` | `configuration-issues` | Config file validation |
104: 
105: ### Auto-Registration
106: 
107: Rules self-register using the `inventory` crate. No manual editing of `lib.rs` registration arrays is needed. Each rule module adds at the bottom:
108: 
109: ```rust
110: inventory::submit!(crate::RuleRegistration::new("RULE_ID", RuleStruct::from_config));
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Configuration System
114: 
115: Config file: `.mlt.toml` (discovered in CWD, or explicit `--config <path>`).
116: 
117: ```toml
118: [lint]
119: exclude = ["vendor/**"]
120: 
121: [lint.categories]
122: performance = "off"          # Disable all performance rules
123: compatibility = "warn"       # Set all compatibility rules to warning
124: 
125: [lint.rules]
126: NOSEMI = "info"              # Shorthand: severity only
127: AGROW = "off"               # Disable rule
128: 
129: [lint.rules.NOSEMI]          # Full table: severity + rule-specific params
130: severity = "error"
131: ignore_functions = ["disp", "fprintf"]
132: ```
133: 
134: Resolution order: per-rule > per-category > rule default.
135: 
136: Rules access typed parameters via `config.rule_params::<T>(rule_id)`, which deserializes the rule's TOML table into a `#[derive(Deserialize, Default)]` struct.
137: 
138: ## Adding a New Rule
139: 
140: This is the most common task. Follow these steps exactly:
141: 
142: ### 1. Create the rule module
143: 
144: Create `crates/mlt_rules/src/<rule_id_lowercase>.rs`:
145: 
146: ```rust
147: //! # RULE_ID: Rule Description
148: //!
149: //! Explanation of what the rule checks.
150: 
151: use mlt_core::{Category, Config, Diagnostic, Fix, NodeContext, Rule, Severity};
152: use serde::Deserialize;
153: 
154: /// Rule-specific configuration (deserialized from .mlt.toml).
155: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Default)]
156: pub struct RuleIdConfig {
157:     // Add rule-specific parameters here with #[serde(default)]
158: }
159: 
160: pub struct RuleId {
161:     config: RuleIdConfig,
162: }
163: 
164: impl RuleId {
165:     pub fn from_config(config: &Config) -> Box<dyn Rule> {
166:         let rule_config: RuleIdConfig = config.rule_params("RULE_ID");
167:         Box::new(Self { config: rule_config })
168:     }
169: }
170: 
171: impl Rule for RuleId {
172:     fn id(&self) -> &'static str { "RULE_ID" }
173:     fn description(&self) -> &'static str { "..." }
174:     fn severity(&self) -> Severity { Severity::Warning }
175:     fn category(&self) -> Category { Category::GoodPractices }
176:     fn target_node_types(&self) -> &'static [&'static str] { &["..."] }
177: 
178:     fn check(&self, ctx: &NodeContext) -> Vec<Diagnostic> {
179:         // Implementation here
180:         Vec::new()
181:     }
182: }
183: 
184: inventory::submit!(crate::RuleRegistration::new("RULE_ID", RuleId::from_config));
185: ```
186: 
187: ### 2. Register the module
188: 
189: In `crates/mlt_rules/src/lib.rs`, add only:
190: 
191: ```rust
192: pub mod rule_id_lowercase;
193: ```
194: 
195: No other changes needed — `inventory` handles the rest.
196: 
197: ### 3. Add documentation
198: 
199: Create `docs/<rule_id_lowercase>.md` following the format of `docs/nosemi.md`:
200: 
201: - Title with rule ID and name
202: - Default severity, auto-fix status, category, can-be-disabled
203: - "What this rule does" section
204: - "Why this matters" section
205: - Examples: Correct / Incorrect / Fixed (with MATLAB code blocks)
206: - Configuration table with parameters
207: - Automatic fixes description
208: - Target node types
209: - Related rules
210: 
211: ### 4. Update docs/rules.md
212: 
213: Add a row to the rule table in `docs/rules.md`.
214: 
215: ### 5. Update zensical.toml nav
216: 
217: Add the rule page to the `Rules` section in `zensical.toml`:
218: 
219: ```toml
220: { "RULE_ID - Name" = "rule_id_lowercase.md" },
221: ```
222: 
223: ### 6. Verify
224: 
225: ```bash
226: cargo build
227: cargo clippy
228: cargo test
229: ```
230: 
231: ## Key Patterns and Conventions
232: 
233: ### Rule ID Convention
234: 
235: Rule IDs match MATLAB Code Analyzer check IDs exactly (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `PFBNS`, `naming.class.casing`). This gives users familiar IDs and enables feature parity tracking.
236: 
237: ### Data-Driven Rules
238: 
239: For large groups of similar checks (Compatibility: ~1800, Suggested Improvements: ~243), use data-driven lookup tables:
240: 
241: ```rust
242: // Load from embedded TOML data file
243: const DATA: &str = include_str!("data/compatibility.toml");
244: ```
245: 
246: A single rule module handles many check IDs by matching function names against a lookup table.
247: 
248: ### Generic Rule Engines
249: 
250: For systematic patterns (Naming: 81 checks = 9 entities x 9 check types), implement a single generic engine parameterized by configuration.
251: 
252: ### Tree-sitter Node Types
253: 
254: The MATLAB grammar (tree-sitter-matlab 1.3) defines these important node types:
255: 
256: - **Statements**: `assignment`, `function_call`, `command`, `for_statement`, `if_statement`, `while_statement`, `switch_statement`, `try_statement`, `return_statement`, `break_statement`, `continue_statement`
257: - **Expressions**: `binary_operator`, `boolean_operator`, `comparison_operator`, `unary_operator`, `postfix_operator`, `number`, `string`, `identifier`, `function_call`, `field_expression`, `cell`, `matrix`, `range`, `lambda`
258: - **Structural**: `source_file`, `block`, `function_definition`, `class_definition`, `properties`, `methods`, `arguments_statement`
259: - **OOP**: `attributes`, `attribute`, `enumeration`, `enum`, `events`, `property`, `superclasses`
260: - **Statement parents**: `source_file`, `block` (use these to determine if a node is at statement level)
261: 
262: **Important limitation**: `function_call` is used for both actual function calls AND array/cell indexing. The grammar cannot distinguish them.
263: 
264: ### Checking Statement-Level Context
265: 
266: Many rules need to know if a node is a statement (top-level in a block) vs. a sub-expression. Pattern:
267: 
268: ```rust
269: let is_statement_level = node
270:     .parent()
271:     .map(|p| ["source_file", "block"].contains(&p.kind()))
272:     .unwrap_or(false);
273: ```
274: 
275: ### Fix Construction
276: 
277: ```rust
278: // Simple insertion
279: Fix::insert(byte_offset, ";")
280: 
281: // Replacement
282: Fix::new(start..end, "replacement_text")
283: 
284: // Multi-edit (atomic)
285: Fix::with_additional(primary_range, primary_replacement, vec![
286:     Fix::new(other_range, other_replacement),
287: ])
288: ```
289: 
290: ### Rule Config Pattern
291: 
292: Every rule should define a `#[derive(Deserialize, Default)]` config struct, even if currently empty. This makes adding parameters non-breaking:
293: 
294: ```rust
295: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Default)]
296: pub struct RuleIdConfig {
297:     #[serde(default)]
298:     pub some_param: Vec<String>,
299: }
300: ```
301: 
302: ## Commands
303: 
304: | Command | Purpose |
305: |---------|---------|
306: | `cargo build` | Build all crates |
307: | `cargo clippy` | Lint Rust code (must pass with zero warnings) |
308: | `cargo test` | Run all tests (unit tests in `mlt_core::config`) |
309: | `cargo run -- <file.m>` | Run the linter on a MATLAB file |
310: | `cargo run -- --fix <file.m>` | Apply auto-fixes |
311: | `cargo run -- --config path/.mlt.toml <file.m>` | Lint with explicit config |
312: 
313: ## Quality Standards
314: 
315: - Zero clippy warnings (CI gate)
316: - All public types and functions must have doc comments
317: - Rule modules must have module-level `//!` documentation with examples
318: - Every rule must have a corresponding `docs/<rule_id>.md` documentation page
319: - Tests should cover: rule fires correctly, rule does NOT fire on valid code, config parameters are respected
320: 
321: ## Documentation System
322: 
323: Documentation uses [Zensical](https://zensical.org) (successor to Material for MkDocs):
324: 
325: - Config: `zensical.toml` at repo root
326: - Content: `docs/` directory (Markdown)
327: - Preview: `zensical serve` (requires `pip install zensical`)
328: - Build: `zensical build`
329: 
330: ### Documentation Structure
331: 
332: ```
333: docs/
334: ├── index.md                    # Landing page
335: ├── getting-started/
336: │   ├── installation.md         # How to install
337: │   └── quickstart.md           # Basic usage
338: ├── usage/
339: │   ├── cli.md                  # CLI reference
340: │   ├── editors.md              # Editor integration
341: │   └── ci-cd.md                # CI/CD integration
342: ├── configuration.md            # .mlt.toml schema reference
343: ├── rules.md                    # Rules overview + table
344: └── <rule_id>.md                # One page per rule (flat, not nested)
345: ```
346: 
347: ### Rule Documentation Template
348: 
349: Every rule page follows this structure (see `docs/nosemi.md` as the canonical example):
350: 
351: 1. `# RULE_ID - <Human Name>`
352: 2. Default severity + auto-fix badge + category + can-be-disabled
353: 3. "What this rule does"
354: 4. "Why this matters" (bullet points)
355: 5. "Examples" → Correct / Incorrect / Fixed (MATLAB code blocks)
356: 6. "Configuration" (TOML example + parameters table)
357: 7. "Automatic fixes" (describe what the fix does)
358: 8. "Target node types" (tree-sitter nodes)
359: 9. "Related rules"

(End of file - total 359 lines)
</content>

1: # PLAN.md — MATLAB Code Analyzer Feature Parity for mlt
2: 
3: This document tracks the implementation plan for bringing mlt to full feature
4: parity with MATLAB's Code Analyzer (~2,680 checks).
5: 
6: **Decisions made:**
7: - Rule IDs match MATLAB's native check IDs exactly (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `naming.class.casing`).
8: - Compatibility/behavior-change checks (~1,800) use a data-driven TOML lookup table.
9: - Naming checks (81) use a single generic engine with 81 separate rule IDs.
10: - Custom checks (25) use a single engine with per-check thresholds.
11: - Rules auto-register via the `inventory` crate — no manual `lib.rs` arrays.
12: - Category-level config is supported (`[lint.categories]` in `.mlt.toml`).
13: 
14: ---
15:

23: | Compatibility | `compatibility.rs` + `data/compatibility.toml` | ~275 (of 323 entries; 48 are generic/unfilled) | Data-driven HashMap lookup |

133: ## Phase 1: Data-Driven Rule Engines ✅ COMPLETE
134: 
135: ### 1.1 — Compatibility Lookup Engine ✅
136: - **File:** `crates/mlt_rules/src/compatibility.rs` (245 lines)
137: - **Data:** `crates/mlt_rules/src/data/compatibility.toml` (323 entries, 2,350 lines)
138: - Single `CompatibilityEngine` targeting `function_call` and `command` nodes.
139: - `LazyLock<HashMap>` built from TOML at first access; O(1) lookup per function name.
140: - Diagnostics carry the specific MATLAB check ID (e.g., `DPSD`), not the meta-ID.

142: - **48 entries** are generic (empty `function_name`); require future AST pattern matching.

146: ### 1.2 — Generic Naming Engine ✅
147: - **File:** `crates/mlt_rules/src/naming.rs` (849 lines)
148: - Single `NamingEngine` registered as file-level rule.
149: - Generates 81 static rule IDs (`naming.<entity>.<checkType>`).

2: //!
3: //! This module implements 7 formatting checks from MATLAB's Code Analyzer as
4: //! a single file-level rule engine. The checks are:

6: //! | Check ID | Description |
7: //! |----------|-------------|

9: //! | NO4LP    | Use 4-space indentation in loop/conditional bodies |
10: //! | ALIGN    | Code alignment suggestion (elseif/else vs. if) |
11: //! | NOPTS    | Add parentheses around condition in if/while |

14: //! | NCOMMA   | Use comma to separate input arguments |

# Quickstart for stacked pull requests

Install the gh stack extension in GitHub CLI and create your first set of stacked pull requests.

> \[!NOTE] This feature is in public preview and subject to change.

Use stacked pull requests to break large code changes into a chain of smaller, dependent pull requests that you can review and merge independently.

A stack is a series of pull requests in the same repository where each pull request targets the branch of the pull request below it, forming an ordered chain that lands on a single branch, typically your main branch. Instead of one large pull request, you get a set of smaller pull requests. Since each pull request has its own focused diff, teammates can review and approve each layer independently.

## Prerequisites

* GitHub CLI (`gh`) 2.90.0 or later, and Git 2.20 or later.
  * Authenticate GitHub CLI with `gh auth login`.
* A GitHub repository you can push to.

## Install the CLI extension

```shell copy
gh extension install github/gh-stack
```

> \[!TIP]
> To use stacked pull requests with AI coding agents, like GitHub Copilot, install the `gh-stack` skill.
>
> ```shell copy
> gh skill install github/gh-stack
> ```

## Create your first stack

1. To initialize a stack, navigate to your repository and run the following command. This creates a tracking entry and your first branch.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack init
   ```

   You'll be prompted to name your first branch. By default, the stack uses your repository's default branch (e.g., `main`) as the trunk, but a stack can target any branch.

2. Work on your first branch as usual: write code, stage changes, and commit.

   ```shell
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "helpful-commit-message"
   ```

3. When you're ready for the next logical unit of work, add a new branch to the top of the stack.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "Another-helpful-commit-message"
   ```

4. Push all branches to the remote.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack push
   ```

5. Create pull requests and link them as a stack on GitHub.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack submit
   ```

   Each pull request is created with the correct base branch. Your first branch targets `main`, and the next branch `BRANCH-NAME` targets the first branch. Reviewers will only see the diff for that layer. The pull requests are automatically linked together as a stack on GitHub and you can see their order and quickly navigate between them.

6. View the stack and see the full state at any time.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack view
   ```

   This command shows all branches, their pull request links, statuses, and the most recent commit on each.

7. Use `gh stack add -Am "MESSAGE"` to stage all changes, commit, and create the next branch in one step. You won't need a separate `git add` or `git commit`. If the current branch has no commits yet, the commit lands there; if it already has commits, a new branch is created.

   ```shell
   # Commit lands on the current branch
   gh stack add -Am "Auth middleware"

   # Current branch already has commits, so this creates the next branch
   gh stack add -Am "API routes"
   ```

8. When you're ready, push everything and create the pull requests.

   ```shell copy
   gh stack submit
   ```

## Next steps

* [Managing stacked pull requests](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/managing-stacked-pull-requests)
* [Merging stacked pull requests](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/merging-stacked-pull-requests)
* [Stack AI-generated code in pull requests](/en/copilot/tutorials/stack-ai-generated-code-in-pull-requests)
* [Roll out stacked pull requests to your organization](/en/pull-requests/tutorials/roll-out-stacked-prs)

## Development Workflow: Stacked PRs

This repository uses **stacked pull requests** to land changes as a chain of
small, reviewable PRs. Each PR targets the branch of the PR below it, forming
an ordered stack that lands on `feat`.

### Setup (once per machine)

Install the `gh stack` extension and authenticate:

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-stack
gh auth login
```

### Daily flow

1. Start a stack from the trunk (`feat`):

   ```bash
   gh stack init          # prompts for the first branch name
   ```

2. Work on the current branch, then stage + commit:

   ```bash
   git add .
   git commit -m "helpful message"
   ```

3. Add the next logical unit of work on top of the stack:

   ```bash
   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME        # new branch on top
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "next unit"
   ```

   branch in a single step.

4. Push everything and open the linked PRs:

   ```bash
   gh stack push
   gh stack submit
   ```

5. Inspect the stack state:

   ```bash
   gh stack view
   ```

### Conventions

- **Trunk:** `feat` (this repo's integration branch).

## Development Workflow: Stacked Pull Requests

This repository uses **stacked pull requests** to land changes as a chain of
small, independently reviewable PRs instead of one large PR. Each PR targets
the branch of the PR below it, forming an ordered stack that lands on `feat`.

See the [GitHub stacked PRs quickstart](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/stacked-prs-quickstart)
for the official guide.

### Setup (once per machine)

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-stack
gh auth login
```

Requires `gh` ≥ 2.90 and Git ≥ 2.20.

### Daily flow

1. **Start a stack** from the trunk (`feat`):

   ```bash
   gh stack init            # prompts for the first branch name
   ```

   To turn existing branches into a stack, list them in dependency order:

   ```bash
   gh stack init feat/clippy-warnings feat/formatting-checks feat/plan-update
   ```

2. **Work and commit** on the current branch:

   ```bash
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "helpful message"
   ```

3. **Add the next logical unit** on top of the stack:

   ```bash
   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "next unit"
   ```

   Or stage, commit, and branch in one step:

   ```bash
   gh stack add -Am "next unit"
   ```

4. **Push and submit** the PRs (each PR is auto-linked to its base branch):

   ```bash
   gh stack push
   gh stack submit
   ```

5. **Inspect the stack** at any time:

   ```bash
   gh stack view
   ```

### Conventions

- **Trunk:** `feat` is this repo's integration branch; the bottom PR of every
  stack targets it.
- **One logical unit per branch.** Split work so each branch is independently
  reviewable — e.g., one branch for clippy cleanups, the next for a rule
  engine plus its tests, and docs/plan updates on top.
- **Keep stacks shallow** (2–4 branches). Deep stacks are hard to review and
  prone to merge conflicts.
- **Review and merge bottom-up.** Each PR's diff shrinks as its dependencies
  land, keeping downstream PRs small.
- **Sync with trunk** before merging: rebase the bottom branch onto `feat`,
  then each branch onto its parent.

+   ```
+
+2. **Work and commit** on the current branch:
+
+   ```bash
+   # ... write code ...
+   git add .
+   git commit -m "helpful message"
+   ```
+
+3. **Add the next logical unit** on top of the stack:
+
+   ```bash
+   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
+   # ... write code ...
+   git add .
+   git commit -m "next unit"
+   ```
+
+   Or stage, commit, and branch in one step:
+
+   ```bash
+   gh stack add -Am "next unit"
+   ```
+
+4. **Push and submit** the PRs (each PR is auto-linked to its base branch):
+
+   ```bash
+   gh stack push
+   gh stack submit
+   ```
+
+5. **Inspect the stack** at any time:
+
+   ```bash
+   gh stack view
+   ```
+
+### Conventions
+
+- **Trunk:** `feat` is this repo's integration branch; the bottom PR of every
+  stack targets it.
+- **One logical unit per branch.** Split work so each branch is independently
+  reviewable — e.g., one branch for clippy cleanups, the next for a rule
+  engine plus its tests, and docs/plan updates on top.
+- **Keep stacks shallow** (2–4 branches). Deep stacks are hard to review and
+  prone to merge conflicts.
+- **Review and merge bottom-up.** Each PR's diff shrinks as its dependencies
+  land, keeping downstream PRs small.
+- **Sync with trunk** before merging: rebase the bottom branch onto `feat`,
+  then each branch onto its parent.

# PLAN.md — MATLAB Code Analyzer Feature Parity for mlt

This document tracks the implementation plan for bringing mlt to full feature
parity with MATLAB's Code Analyzer (~2,680 checks).

**Decisions made:**
- Rule IDs match MATLAB's native check IDs exactly (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `naming.class.casing`).
- Compatibility/behavior-change checks (~1,800) use a data-driven TOML lookup table.
- Naming checks (81) use a single generic engine with 81 separate rule IDs.
- Custom checks (25) use a single engine with per-check thresholds.
- Rules auto-register via the `inventory` crate — no manual `lib.rs` arrays.
- Category-level config is supported (`[lint.categories]` in `.mlt.toml`).

## Development Workflow: Stacked Pull Requests

This repository uses **stacked pull requests** to land changes as a chain of
small, independently reviewable PRs instead of one large PR. Each PR targets
the branch of the PR below it, forming an ordered stack that lands on `feat`.

See the [GitHub stacked PRs quickstart](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/stacked-prs-quickstart)
for the official guide.

### Setup (once per machine)

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-stack
gh auth login
```

Requires `gh` ≥ 2.90 and Git ≥ 2.20.

### Daily flow

1. **Start a stack** from the trunk (`feat`):

   ```bash
   gh stack init --base feat        # prompts for the first branch name
   ```

   To turn existing branches into a stack, list them in dependency order:

   ```bash
   gh stack init --base feat feature/foo feature/bar feature/baz
   ```

2. **Work and commit** on the current branch:

   ```bash
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "helpful message"
   ```

3. **Add the next logical unit** on top of the stack:

   ```bash
   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "next unit"
   ```

   Or stage, commit, and branch in one step:

   ```bash
   gh stack add -Am "next unit"
   ```

4. **Push and submit** the PRs (each PR is auto-linked to its base branch):

   ```bash
   gh stack push
   gh stack submit
   ```

5. **Inspect the stack** at any time:

   ```bash
   gh stack view
   ```

### Conventions

- **Trunk:** `feat` is this repo's integration branch; the bottom PR of every
  stack targets it.
- **One logical unit per branch.** Split work so each branch is independently
  reviewable — e.g., one branch for clippy cleanups, the next for a rule
  engine plus its tests, and docs/plan updates on top.
- **Keep stacks shallow** (2–4 branches). Deep stacks are hard to review and
  prone to merge conflicts.
- **Review and merge bottom-up.** Each PR's diff shrinks as its dependencies
  land, keeping downstream PRs small.
- **Sync with trunk** before merging: rebase the bottom branch onto `feat`,
  then each branch onto its parent.

locally, then push to GitHub to create your stack of PRs.

Usage:
  gh stack [command]

Examples:
  # Start a new stack targeting your default branch
  $ gh stack init

  # Or turn an existing set of branches into a stack
  $ gh stack init branch1 branch2 branch3

  # Make changes and commit, then add a branch to the stack
  $ gh stack add branch4

  # Push all branches and create/update PRs on GitHub
  $ gh stack submit

  # Keep your local in sync with remote
  $ gh stack sync

Stack management:
  add         Add a new branch on top of the current stack
  checkout    Checkout a stack by stack number, PR number, PR URL, or branch name
  init        Initialize a new stack
  modify      Interactively restructure a stack
  unstack     Remove a stack locally and on GitHub
  view        View the current stack

1: # PLAN.md — MATLAB Code Analyzer Feature Parity for mlt
2: 
3: This document tracks the implementation plan for bringing mlt to full feature
4: parity with MATLAB's Code Analyzer (~2,680 checks).
5: 
6: **Decisions made:**
7: - Rule IDs match MATLAB's native check IDs exactly (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `naming.class.casing`).
8: - Compatibility/behavior-change checks (~1,800) use a data-driven TOML lookup table.
9: - Naming checks (81) use a single generic engine with 81 separate rule IDs.
10: - Custom checks (25) use a single engine with per-check thresholds.
11: - Rules auto-register via the `inventory` crate — no manual `lib.rs` arrays.
12: - Category-level config is supported (`[lint.categories]` in `.mlt.toml`).
13: - Changes land via **stacked pull requests** (see below).
14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ## Development Workflow: Stacked Pull Requests
18: 
19: This repository uses **stacked pull requests** to land changes as a chain of
20: small, independently reviewable PRs instead of one large PR. Each PR targets
21: the branch of the PR below it, forming an ordered stack that lands on `feat`.
22: 
23: See the [GitHub stacked PRs quickstart](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/stacked-prs-quickstart)
24: for the official guide.
25: 
26: ### Setup (once per machine)
27: 
28: ```bash
29: gh extension install github/gh-stack
30: gh auth login
31: ```
32: 
33: Requires `gh` ≥ 2.90 and Git ≥ 2.20.
34: 
35: ### Daily flow
36: 
37: 1. **Start a stack** from the trunk (`feat`):
38: 
39:    ```bash
40:    gh stack init --base feat        # prompts for the first branch name
41:    ```
42: 
43:    To turn existing branches into a stack, list them in dependency order:
44: 
45:    ```bash
46:    gh stack init --base feat feature/foo feature/bar feature/baz
47:    ```
48: 
49: 2. **Work and commit** on the current branch:
50: 
51:    ```bash
52:    # ... write code ...
53:    git add .
54:    git commit -m "helpful message"
55:    ```
56: 
57: 3. **Add the next logical unit** on top of the stack:
58: 
59:    ```bash
60:    gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
61:    # ... write code ...
62:    git add .
63:    git commit -m "next unit"
64:    ```
65: 
66:    Or stage, commit, and branch in one step:
67: 
68:    ```bash
69:    gh stack add -Am "next unit"
70:    ```
71: 
72: 4. **Push and submit** the PRs (each PR is auto-linked to its base branch):
73: 
74:    ```bash
75:    gh stack push
76:    gh stack submit
77:    ```
78: 
79: 5. **Inspect the stack** at any time:
80: 
81:    ```bash
82:    gh stack view
83:    ```
84: 
85: ### Conventions
86: 
87: - **Trunk:** `feat` is this repo's integration branch; the bottom PR of every
88:   stack targets it.
89: - **One logical unit per branch.** Split work so each branch is independently
90:   reviewable — e.g., one branch for clippy cleanups, the next for a rule
91:   engine plus its tests, and docs/plan updates on top.
92: - **Keep stacks shallow** (2–4 branches). Deep stacks are hard to review and
93:   prone to merge conflicts.
94: - **Review and merge bottom-up.** Each PR's diff shrinks as its dependencies
95:   land, keeping downstream PRs small.
96: - **Sync with trunk** before merging: rebase the bottom branch onto `feat`,
97:   then each branch onto its parent.

This document tracks the implementation plan for bringing mlt to full feature
parity with MATLAB's Code Analyzer (~2,680 checks).

**Decisions made:**
- Rule IDs match MATLAB's native check IDs exactly (e.g., `NOSEMI`, `AGROW`, `naming.class.casing`).
- Compatibility/behavior-change checks (~1,800) use a data-driven TOML lookup table.
- Naming checks (81) use a single generic engine with 81 separate rule IDs.
- Custom checks (25) use a single engine with per-check thresholds.

## Development Workflow: Stacked Pull Requests

This repository uses **stacked pull requests** to land changes as a chain of
small, independently reviewable PRs instead of one large PR. Each PR targets
the branch of the PR below it, forming an ordered stack that lands on `feat`.

See the [GitHub stacked PRs quickstart](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/stacked-prs-quickstart)
for the official guide.

### Setup (once per machine)

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-stack
gh auth login
```

Requires `gh` ≥ 2.90 and Git ≥ 2.20.

### Daily flow

1. **Start a stack** from the trunk (`feat`):

   ```bash
   gh stack init --base feat        # prompts for the first branch name
   ```

   To turn existing branches into a stack, list them in dependency order:

   ```bash
   gh stack init --base feat feature/foo feature/bar feature/baz
   ```

2. **Work and commit** on the current branch:

   ```bash
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "helpful message"
   ```

3. **Add the next logical unit** on top of the stack:

   ```bash
   gh stack add BRANCH-NAME
   # ... write code ...
   git add .
   git commit -m "next unit"
   ```

   Or stage, commit, and branch in one step:

   ```bash
   gh stack add -Am "next unit"
   ```

4. **Push and submit** the PRs (each PR is auto-linked to its base branch):

   ```bash
   gh stack push
   gh stack submit
   ```

5. **Inspect the stack** at any time:

   ```bash
   gh stack view
   ```

### Conventions

- **Trunk:** `feat` is this repo's integration branch; the bottom PR of every
  stack targets it.
- **One logical unit per branch.** Split work so each branch is independently
  reviewable — e.g., one branch for clippy cleanups, the next for a rule
  engine plus its tests, and docs/plan updates on top.
- **Keep stacks shallow** (2–4 branches). Deep stacks are hard to review and
  prone to merge conflicts.
- **Review and merge bottom-up.** Each PR's diff shrinks as its dependencies
  land, keeping downstream PRs small.
- **Sync with trunk** before merging: rebase the bottom branch onto `feat`,
  then each branch onto its parent.

1: //! # READABILITY_ENGINE: Readability Improvements
2: //!
3: //! A multi-check rule engine that detects readability improvements in MATLAB
4: //! code. Instead of implementing one struct per check, a single
5: //! `ReadabilityEngine` dispatches to per-check-ID logic inside its `check()`
6: //! method, emitting diagnostics with specific check IDs (e.g., `ISCHR`,
7: //! `IJCL`, `RPMT1`).
8: //!
9: //! ## Checks
10: //!
11: //! This engine covers 35 readability checks across these patterns:
12: //!
13: //! - **Type checking simplification** (ISCHR, ISSTR, ISLOG, ISCEL, ISMAT):
14: //!   prefer `ischar`, `isstring`, etc. over `isa(x, 'type')`.
15: //! - **Dimension checks** (ISROW, ISCOL): prefer `isrow`/`iscolumn` over
16: //!   `size(x,dim)==1`.
17: //! - **Variable shadowing** (IJCL): `i`/`j` as assignment LHS shadows the
18: //!   complex unit.
19: //! - **Unnecessary brackets** (NBRAK2): `[x]` where `x` is a scalar.
20: //! - **String comparisons** (STREMP, STRCL1, STRCLFH, STRIFCND): prefer
21: //!   modern string functions.
22: //! - **Character literals** (CHARTEN): use `newline` instead of `char(10)`.
23: //! - **Formatting** (SPRINTFN): use `num2str` over simple `sprintf`.
24: //! - **Control flow style** (ASGSL): avoid inline assignment in conditions.
25: //! - **Error/warning style** (SPERR, SPWRN): prefer message IDs.
26: //! - **Input validation** (NCHKE): prefer `narginchk`/`nargoutchk`.
27: //! - **Output style** (DSPSP, DSPSY): prefer `fprintf`/`disp` over wrappers.
28: //! - **Path construction** (FLUDLR): prefer `fullfile`.
29: //! - **Redundant arithmetic** (RPMT1, RPMT0, RPMTI, RPMTN): simplify trivial
30: //!   multiplication/addition.
31: //! - **Redundant logic** (RPMTT, RPMTF): simplify boolean tautologies.
32: //! - **Size helpers** (PSIZE): prefer `numel` over `prod(size(x))`.
33: //! - **Logical helpers** (LOGSUM, LOGL): prefer `any`/logical indexing.
34: //!
35: //! ## Configuration
36: //!
37: //! ```toml
38: //! [lint.rules.READABILITY_ENGINE]
39: //! severity = "info"
40: //! disabled_checks = ["IJCL", "NBRAK2"]
41: //! ```

599:     /// PSIZE: `prod(size(x))` → `numel(x)`
600:     fn check_prod_size(
601:         &self,
602:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
603:         source: &str,
604:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
605:     ) {
606:         if !self.is_check_enabled("PSIZE") {
607:             return;
608:         }
609: 
610:         let args = match find_arguments(node) {
611:             Some(a) => a,
612:             None => return,
613:         };
614: 
615:         let named_children: Vec<_> = (0..args.named_child_count())
616:             .filter_map(|i| args.named_child(i))
617:             .collect();
618: 
619:         if named_children.len() != 1 {
620:             return;
621:         }
622: 
623:         let inner = named_children[0];
624:         if inner.kind() == "function_call" {
625:             if let Some(inner_name) = inner.child_by_field_name("name") {
626:                 let inner_func = &source[inner_name.start_byte()..inner_name.end_byte()];
627:                 if inner_func == "size" {
628:                     // Extract the variable passed to size
629:                     if let Some(inner_args) = find_arguments(inner) {
630:                         let inner_named: Vec<_> = (0..inner_args.named_child_count())
631:                             .filter_map(|i| inner_args.named_child(i))
632:                             .collect();
633:                         if inner_named.len() == 1 {
634:                             let var_text = &source
635:                                 [inner_named[0].start_byte()..inner_named[0].end_byte()];
636:                             results.push(self.diag(
637:                                 "PSIZE",
638:                                 "Use 'numel(x)' instead of 'prod(size(x))'",
639:                                 node,
640:                                 Some(Fix::new(
641:                                     node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
642:                                     format!("numel({var_text})"),
643:                                 )),
644:                             ));
645:                         }
646:                     }
647:                 }
648:             }
649:         }
650:     }
651: 
652:     /// LOGSUM: `sum(logical) > 0` → `any(logical)`
653:     ///
654:     /// We detect `function_call` named `sum` and check if it appears as the
655:     /// left-hand side of a `> 0` comparison in the parent node. If no parent
656:     /// comparison is found, we skip (sum alone is fine).
657:     fn check_sum_logical(
658:         &self,
659:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
660:         _source: &str,
661:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
662:     ) {
663:         if !self.is_check_enabled("LOGSUM") {
664:             return;
665:         }
666: 
667:         // Only flag when parent is a comparison `sum(...) > 0`
668:         if let Some(parent) = node.parent() {
669:             if parent.kind() == "comparison_operator" {
670:                 results.push(self.diag(
671:                     "LOGSUM",
672:                     "Consider using 'any(...)' instead of 'sum(...) > 0'",
673:                     parent,
674:                     None,
675:                 ));
676:             }
677:         }
678:     }
679: 
680:     /// LOGL: `x(find(condition))` → `x(condition)`
681:     ///
682:     /// Detects `find` as an argument to array/cell indexing. Since tree-sitter
683:     /// cannot distinguish `f(x)` from `a(i)`, we flag `find` calls used as
684:     /// arguments inside any `function_call` parent, which is the typical
685:     /// indexing pattern.
686:     fn check_find_logical(
687:         &self,
688:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
689:         _source: &str,
690:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
691:     ) {
692:         if !self.is_check_enabled("LOGL") {
693:             return;
694:         }
695: 
696:         // find() used as argument inside another function_call (array indexing)
697:         if let Some(parent) = node.parent() {
698:             // The parent of the function_call `find(...)` should be an
699:             // arguments node, and *its* parent should be a function_call
700:             if let Some(grandparent) = parent.parent() {
701:                 if grandparent.kind() == "function_call" {
702:                     results.push(self.diag(
703:                         "LOGL",
704:                         "Use logical indexing 'x(condition)' instead of 'x(find(condition))'",
705:                         node,
706:                         None,
707:                     ));
708:                 }
709:             }
710:         }
711:     }

713:     /// ISROW / ISCOL: `size(x, dim) == 1` patterns
714:     fn check_size_comparison(
715:         &self,
716:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
717:         source: &str,
718:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
719:     ) {
720:         // We need at least 3 children: lhs, operator, rhs
721:         if node.named_child_count() < 2 {
722:             return;
723:         }
724: 
725:         // Get the comparison operator text
726:         let node_text = &source[node.start_byte()..node.end_byte()];
727:         if !node_text.contains("==") {
728:             return;
729:         }
730: 
731:         // Find a function_call to `size` in the children
732:         let mut size_call = None;
733:         let mut other_side = None;
734: 
735:         for i in 0..node.named_child_count() {
736:             if let Some(child) = node.named_child(i) {
737:                 if child.kind() == "function_call" {
738:                     if let Some(name_node) = child.child_by_field_name("name") {
739:                         let name = &source[name_node.start_byte()..name_node.end_byte()];
740:                         if name == "size" {
741:                             size_call = Some(child);
742:                             continue;
743:                         }
744:                     }
745:                 }
746:                 other_side = Some(child);
747:             }
748:         }
749: 
750:         let size_node = match size_call {
751:             Some(n) => n,
752:             None => return,
753:         };
754: 
755:         // Check the "other side" is `1`
756:         let other = match other_side {
757:             Some(n) => n,
758:             None => return,
759:         };
760:         let other_text = &source[other.start_byte()..other.end_byte()].trim();
761:         if *other_text != "1" {
762:             return;
763:         }
764: 
765:         // Extract the dimension argument from size(x, dim)
766:         let args = match find_arguments(size_node) {
767:             Some(a) => a,
768:             None => return,
769:         };
770: 
771:         let named_children: Vec<_> = (0..args.named_child_count())
772:             .filter_map(|i| args.named_child(i))
773:             .collect();
774: 
775:         if named_children.len() != 2 {
776:             return;
777:         }
778: 
779:         let var_text = &source[named_children[0].start_byte()..named_children[0].end_byte()];
780:         let dim_text = &source[named_children[1].start_byte()..named_children[1].end_byte()].trim();
781: 
782:         match *dim_text {
783:             "1" if self.is_check_enabled("ISROW") => {
784:                 results.push(self.diag(
785:                     "ISROW",
786:                     "Use 'isrow(x)' instead of 'size(x, 1) == 1'",
787:                     node,
788:                     Some(Fix::new(
789:                         node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
790:                         format!("isrow({var_text})"),
791:                     )),
792:                 ));
793:             }
794:             "2" if self.is_check_enabled("ISCOL") => {
795:                 results.push(self.diag(
796:                     "ISCOL",
797:                     "Use 'iscolumn(x)' instead of 'size(x, 2) == 1'",
798:                     node,
799:                     Some(Fix::new(
800:                         node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
801:                         format!("iscolumn({var_text})"),
802:                     )),
803:                 ));
804:             }
805:             _ => {}
806:         }
807:     }

809:     /// IJCL: Assignment to `i` or `j` shadows the complex unit.
810:     fn check_ij_shadow(
811:         &self,
812:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
813:         source: &str,
814:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
815:     ) {
816:         if !self.is_check_enabled("IJCL") {
817:             return;
818:         }
819: 
820:         // The LHS of an assignment — the first named child or field "left"
821:         let lhs = match node.child_by_field_name("left") {
822:             Some(n) => n,
823:             None => {
824:                 // Fallback: first named child
825:                 match node.named_child(0) {
826:                     Some(n) => n,
827:                     None => return,
828:                 }
829:             }
830:         };
831: 
832:         if lhs.kind() != "identifier" {
833:             return;
834:         }
835: 
836:         let lhs_text = &source[lhs.start_byte()..lhs.end_byte()];
837:         if lhs_text == "i" || lhs_text == "j" {
838:             results.push(self.diag(
839:                 "IJCL",
840:                 &format!(
841:                     "Variable '{lhs_text}' shadows the built-in complex unit. \
842:                      Use '1i' or '1j' for complex numbers, or rename the variable."
843:                 ),
844:                 lhs,
845:                 None,
846:             ));
847:         }
848:     }

850:     /// ASGSL: Assignment inside a control-flow condition.
851:     fn check_inline_assignment(
852:         &self,
853:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
854:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
855:     ) {
856:         if !self.is_check_enabled("ASGSL") {
857:             return;
858:         }
859: 
860:         // Walk ancestors to see if this assignment is inside a condition
861:         let mut current = node.parent();
862:         while let Some(parent) = current {
863:             match parent.kind() {
864:                 "if_statement" | "while_statement" | "for_statement" => {
865:                     // Check if the assignment is in the condition part
866:                     // (first child of if/while, second child of for)
867:                     results.push(self.diag(
868:                         "ASGSL",
869:                         "Avoid assignment inside control-flow condition; \
870:                          assign on a separate line for clarity",
871:                         node,
872:                         None,
873:                     ));
874:                     return;
875:                 }
876:                 "block" | "source_file" | "function_definition" => {
877:                     // Reached a block boundary — not in a condition
878:                     return;
879:                 }
880:                 _ => {
881:                     current = parent.parent();
882:                 }
883:             }
884:         }
885:     }

887:     /// NBRAK2: Unnecessary brackets `[x]` for scalar expression.
888:     fn check_unnecessary_brackets(
889:         &self,
890:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
891:         source: &str,
892:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
893:     ) {
894:         if !self.is_check_enabled("NBRAK2") {
895:             return;
896:         }
897: 
898:         // A matrix node with exactly one named child that is a "row" with
899:         // exactly one element is `[scalar]`.
900:         let named_count = node.named_child_count();
901:         if named_count != 1 {
902:             return;
903:         }
904: 
905:         let row = match node.named_child(0) {
906:             Some(r) => r,
907:             None => return,
908:         };
909: 
910:         // The row should have exactly one named child (the scalar expression)
911:         if row.kind() == "row" && row.named_child_count() == 1 {
912:             if let Some(inner) = row.named_child(0) {
913:                 // Don't flag complex expressions or function calls that might
914:                 // rely on concatenation behavior
915:                 if matches!(inner.kind(), "identifier" | "number" | "string") {
916:                     let inner_text = &source[inner.start_byte()..inner.end_byte()];
917:                     results.push(self.diag(
918:                         "NBRAK2",
919:                         "Unnecessary brackets around scalar expression",
920:                         node,
921:                         Some(Fix::new(
922:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
923:                             inner_text.to_string(),
924:                         )),
925:                     ));
926:                 }
927:             }
928:         }
929:     }

931:     /// RPMTT, RPMTF: Boolean tautologies `x | true` → `true`, `x & false` → `false`
932:     fn check_boolean_tautology(
933:         &self,
934:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
935:         source: &str,
936:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
937:     ) {
938:         // Need at least: lhs, operator_token, rhs
939:         if node.child_count() < 3 {
940:             return;
941:         }
942: 
943:         // Extract the operator token (unnamed child between named children)
944:         let op_text = extract_operator_text(node, source);
945: 
946:         let (lhs, rhs) = match (node.named_child(0), node.named_child(1)) {
947:             (Some(l), Some(r)) => (l, r),
948:             _ => return,
949:         };
950: 
951:         let lhs_text = &source[lhs.start_byte()..lhs.end_byte()];
952:         let rhs_text = &source[rhs.start_byte()..rhs.end_byte()];
953: 
954:         // x | true → true  OR  true | x → true
955:         if (op_text == "|" || op_text == "||")
956:             && self.is_check_enabled("RPMTT")
957:             && (rhs_text == "true" || lhs_text == "true")
958:         {
959:             results.push(self.diag(
960:                 "RPMTT",
961:                 "Redundant boolean: 'x | true' is always 'true'",
962:                 node,
963:                 Some(Fix::new(node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(), "true")),
964:             ));
965:             return;
966:         }
967: 
968:         // x & false → false  OR  false & x → false
969:         if (op_text == "&" || op_text == "&&")
970:             && self.is_check_enabled("RPMTF")
971:             && (rhs_text == "false" || lhs_text == "false")
972:         {
973:             results.push(self.diag(
974:                 "RPMTF",
975:                 "Redundant boolean: 'x & false' is always 'false'",
976:                 node,
977:                 Some(Fix::new(node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(), "false")),
978:             ));
979:         }
980:     }

982:     /// RPMT1, RPMT0, RPMTI, RPMTN: Redundant arithmetic with constants
983:     fn check_redundant_arithmetic(
984:         &self,
985:         node: tree_sitter::Node,
986:         source: &str,
987:         results: &mut Vec<Diagnostic>,
988:     ) {
989:         if node.child_count() < 3 {
990:             return;
991:         }
992: 
993:         let op_text = extract_operator_text(node, source);
994: 
995:         let (lhs, rhs) = match (node.named_child(0), node.named_child(1)) {
996:             (Some(l), Some(r)) => (l, r),
997:             _ => return,
998:         };
999: 
1000:         let lhs_text = &source[lhs.start_byte()..lhs.end_byte()];
1001:         let rhs_text = &source[rhs.start_byte()..rhs.end_byte()];
1002: 
1003:         match op_text {
1004:             "*" | ".*" => {
1005:                 // RPMT1: x * 1 → x
1006:                 if self.is_check_enabled("RPMT1") && rhs_text == "1" {
1007:                     results.push(self.diag(
1008:                         "RPMT1",
1009:                         "Redundant multiplication by 1; simplify to 'x'",
1010:                         node,
1011:                         Some(Fix::new(
1012:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1013:                             lhs_text.to_string(),
1014:                         )),
1015:                     ));
1016:                     return;
1017:                 }
1018:                 if self.is_check_enabled("RPMT1") && lhs_text == "1" {
1019:                     results.push(self.diag(
1020:                         "RPMT1",
1021:                         "Redundant multiplication by 1; simplify to 'x'",
1022:                         node,
1023:                         Some(Fix::new(
1024:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1025:                             rhs_text.to_string(),
1026:                         )),
1027:                     ));
1028:                     return;
1029:                 }
1030: 
1031:                 // RPMT0: x * 0 → zeros(size(x))
1032:                 if self.is_check_enabled("RPMT0") && rhs_text == "0" {
1033:                     results.push(self.diag(
1034:                         "RPMT0",
1035:                         "Multiplication by 0; consider 'zeros(size(x))' for clarity",
1036:                         node,
1037:                         Some(Fix::new(
1038:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1039:                             format!("zeros(size({lhs_text}))"),
1040:                         )),
1041:                     ));
1042:                 } else if self.is_check_enabled("RPMT0") && lhs_text == "0" {
1043:                     results.push(self.diag(
1044:                         "RPMT0",
1045:                         "Multiplication by 0; consider 'zeros(size(x))' for clarity",
1046:                         node,
1047:                         Some(Fix::new(
1048:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1049:                             format!("zeros(size({rhs_text}))"),
1050:                         )),
1051:                     ));
1052:                 }
1053:             }
1054:             "+" => {
1055:                 // RPMTI: x + 0 → x
1056:                 if self.is_check_enabled("RPMTI") && rhs_text == "0" {
1057:                     results.push(self.diag(
1058:                         "RPMTI",
1059:                         "Redundant addition of 0; simplify to 'x'",
1060:                         node,
1061:                         Some(Fix::new(
1062:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1063:                             lhs_text.to_string(),
1064:                         )),
1065:                     ));
1066:                 } else if self.is_check_enabled("RPMTI") && lhs_text == "0" {
1067:                     results.push(self.diag(
1068:                         "RPMTI",
1069:                         "Redundant addition of 0; simplify to 'x'",
1070:                         node,
1071:                         Some(Fix::new(
1072:                             node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1073:                             rhs_text.to_string(),
1074:                         )),
1075:                     ));
1076:                 }
1077:             }
1078:             "-" if self.is_check_enabled("RPMTN") && rhs_text == "0" => {
1079:                 // RPMTN: x - 0 → x
1080:                 results.push(self.diag(
1081:                     "RPMTN",
1082:                     "Redundant subtraction of 0; simplify to 'x'",
1083:                     node,
1084:                     Some(Fix::new(
1085:                         node.start_byte()..node.end_byte(),
1086:                         lhs_text.to_string(),
1087:                     )),
1088:                 ));
1089:             }
1090:             _ => {}
1091:         }
1092:     }
1093: }

1099: impl Rule for ReadabilityEngine {
1100:     fn id(&self) -> &'static str {
1101:         "READABILITY_ENGINE"
1102:     }
1103: 
1104:     fn description(&self) -> &'static str {
1105:         "Readability improvement checks for MATLAB code"
1106:     }
1107: 
1108:     fn severity(&self) -> Severity {
1109:         Severity::Info
1110:     }
1111: 
1112:     fn category(&self) -> Category {
1113:         Category::Readability
1114:     }
1115: 
1116:     fn target_node_types(&self) -> &'static [&'static str] {
1117:         TARGET_NODES
1118:     }
1119: 
1120:     fn check(&self, ctx: &NodeContext) -> Vec<Diagnostic> {
1121:         let mut results = Vec::new();
1122: 
1123:         match ctx.node.kind() {
1124:             "function_call" => self.check_function_call(ctx, &mut results),
1125:             "comparison_operator" => self.check_comparison(ctx, &mut results),
1126:             "boolean_operator" => self.check_boolean_operator(ctx, &mut results),
1127:             "assignment" => self.check_assignment(ctx, &mut results),
1128:             "binary_operator" => self.check_binary_operator(ctx, &mut results),
1129:             "matrix" => self.check_matrix(ctx, &mut results),
1130:             // `identifier` nodes are handled via `assignment` LHS check (IJCL)
1131:             // rather than standalone identifier dispatch, to avoid false
1132:             // positives on identifier reads.
1133:             _ => {}
1134:         }
1135: 
1136:         results
1137:     }
1138: }

1140: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
1141: // Helpers
1142: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
1143: 
1144: /// Find the `arguments` child of a `function_call` node.
1145: ///
1146: /// In tree-sitter-matlab the call arguments are a child node of kind
1147: /// `arguments` rather than a named field, so `child_by_field_name("arguments")`
1148: /// never matches. This helper locates them by child kind instead.
1149: fn find_arguments(node: tree_sitter::Node) -> Option<tree_sitter::Node> {
1150:     node.named_children(&mut node.walk())
1151:         .find(|c| c.kind() == "arguments")
1152: }
1153: 
1154: /// Check if a string literal represents an empty string (`''` or `""`).
1155: fn is_empty_string(s: &str) -> bool {
1156:     s == "''" || s == "\"\""
1157: }
1158: 
1159: /// Check if a node is inside an `if_statement` condition.
1160: fn is_inside_if_condition(node: tree_sitter::Node) -> bool {
1161:     let mut current = node.parent();
1162:     while let Some(parent) = current {
1163:         match parent.kind() {
1164:             "if_statement" => return true,
1165:             "block" | "source_file" | "function_definition" => return false,
1166:             _ => current = parent.parent(),
1167:         }
1168:     }
1169:     false
1170: }
1171: 
1172: /// Extract the operator text from a binary/boolean operator node.
1173: ///
1174: /// Iterates over unnamed children to find the operator token between operands.
1175: fn extract_operator_text<'a>(node: tree_sitter::Node<'a>, source: &'a str) -> &'a str {
1176:     // Walk all children (including unnamed) looking for the operator
1177:     let mut cursor = node.walk();
1178:     for child in node.children(&mut cursor) {
1179:         if !child.is_named() {
1180:             let text = &source[child.start_byte()..child.end_byte()];
1181:             // Operator tokens are things like +, -, *, .*, |, ||, &, &&, ==
1182:             if !text.trim().is_empty()
1183:                 && text != "("
1184:                 && text != ")"
1185:                 && text != "["
1186:                 && text != "]"
1187:             {
1188:                 return text;
1189:             }
1190:         }
1191:     }
1192:     ""
1193: }

Title: christmas letdown(ton) — Jenny Andrews
URL: http://www.myfavoriteandmybest.com/mfamb/2012/2/22/christmas-letdownton.html
Published: 2012-02-22T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Gabriela Eisenhart
Highlights:
christmas letdown(ton) — Jenny Andrews

Menu

i was expecting more from christmastime at downton.

those snowy images i kept seeing all over the internet were misleading mr. julian fellowes.

christmas lasted 5 minutes then jumped to new years then to a murder trial then to a dog search party then to some hunting then to a snow twirling proposal then to credits.

wait..this whole episode was kind of a letdown.

i am confused by my emotions right now.

i mean i was crying right along with anna when she was going to leave downton.

i was happy to not have to endure more sybil/branson dumbness.

i was moved in a way that only the waltons circa 1980 could move me when daisy realized she loved william and william was the only one who ever really loved her.

and then again moved to tears when william's dad asked to be her dad too.

but the matthew and mary part..

THE MOST IMPORTANT ELEMENT OF THIS SHOW..

was like...huh??

i mean, who doesn't love a snowy twirl?

but..it was a bit anticlimactic if you ask me mr. julian fellowes.

the kiss should have at least made me moist in my unders.

but it didn't.

and i could have done without the rosamund/boyfriend/maid bit.

who cares about that?

no one. that's who.

and i actually felt sorry for carlisle.

he loved mary. he just didn't know how to be cool about it.

he was too possesive and couldn't handle an aloof woman like mary.

plus he looks like this in real life.

so..

i will commence the recap but you should know mr. julian fellowes that next season i won't stand for any more bullshit.

no shark jumping canadian burn victims.

no ouija boards signifying nothing.

no one calling mrs. patmore fat.

unless you called her mrs. fatmore. that would have been hilarious.

i'm kidding, i'm kidding!

seriously that writer needs to be put down like a lame horse.

and..

no more dogs locked in sheds.

etc..

don't get me wrong...

i still LOVED it.

let's go!!

it's christmastime!!

look at the pretty tree with LIGHTS!

it's almost 1920!

the fashions have changed and you can collectively hear all the women shouting.."FUCK YOU SLEEVES!!"

in wintertime no less.

that's so ballsy!

and stupid.

i live in the south where our winters top out at 50 degrees and i am wearing 8 sweaters under my bathrobe all day long.

so while these bitches feign warmth, the servants stand in a line waiting for their gifts.

who planned this condescending shit out?

called forth like they were receiving an award for best cot making abilities.

and

nothing says season finale better than introducing a new storyline and character..

aunt rosamund is at downton for the holidays (but not sybil. weird) and she's brought her sassy mouth new maid..

ms. shaw.

who starts right in with the bates put-downs.

(them's fightin' words!)

and putting ideas into daisy's pea brain about a promotion.

upstairs the gift giving is a bit more civil..albeit still weird..

everyone stands around and opens presents.

stands?

and no where near the tree?

what is wrong with 1919 england?

the DC receives a nutcracker from cousin isobel and matthew.

haha..i get it.

an edwardian gag gift, right?

no???!

then she should have beaten cousin isobel in the eyeball with it.

this whole episode tried to slam down our throats that matthew and mary are sooo right for each other..

while carlisle and mary are soooo not right for each other.

i mean carlisle was lurking in a corner seething with jealousy in virtually every shot.

next up was christmas dinner.

in comes carson with absent sybil's favorite flambe...

downstairs christmas fun means talking to the dead via a ouija board..

while upstairs charades are all the rage..

"charades is gay".

and somewhere not so very christmasy is mr. bates.

sitting in jail wrongfully (or is he??) accused of murdering his wife and awaiting his fate..

i made up a special t-shirt for the occasion...

later on lord grantham confides in carson that he is uncomfortable with the idea of thomas as his new valet.

Title: Brooklyn Limestones Goodies Blog: Nate + Nest + Networking
URL: http://brooklynlimestonegoodies.blogspot.com/2010/10/nate-nest-networking.html
Published: 2026-07-08T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Posted by
 
 Mrs. Limestone
Highlights:
If you follow other design bloggers that attended last Tuesday's Nate Berkus show taping, you've already heard plenty about it. In short - as a result of a twitter and blogging campaign, the Nate Berkus show producers invited a bunch of us to watch a taping. Then HGTV invited us all to lunch at their office (which I am so bummed about the fact I couldnt attend) and then Camila worked with The Nest to throw us a fabulous afterparty.So here is my take on the Nate bit: I did not fly from far away nor did it cost me a great deal to attend so I'm not that upset about it. I think the way it was handled throughout was bad business - we were all herded like cattle in the pre show, no special design bloggy topics that episode, no on air mention of the fact we were even present, no opportunity to meet Nate after the fact, etc - it was kind of foolish of Nate and his producers to let an opportunity for incredibly positive press to leave feeling unfufilled. But hey, who the hell am I? So I'll leave it that. Should you want to read more about check out Sketch42's take on it. If you want to crack up check out MFAMB song parody about it.So enough of the bad stuff...what about the good? Big hand to Camila of High Heeled Foot in the Door and the wonderful women at The Nest who threw us a little bash after the show was over. That was absolutely the highlight of the whole experience because I got to meet sooooo many other amazing bloggers that I've been following for years. It was a giant love fest. (If it weren't for the Nate show I would have never gotten an opportunity to connect with these fabulous people so even if it was an unintentional side effect, points to Nate Berkus for that one.)I also got to meet the event photographer who is an incredible talent and nice guy - Trent Bailey. His portfolio makes me want to throw a fabulous gala event just so he can photograph it. (that's totally normal right?) He was kind enough to share some photos of the party with me so I could share them with you. Trent Bailey Photography-The Nest 00196 by MrsLimestone, on Flickr Trent Bailey Photography-The Nest 00059 by MrsLimestone, on Flickr Some of the lovely ladies I got to chat up: Amy of ABCD Design; Tamara of Get it Girl Style; Emily A Clark; Erika of Blu Label Bungalow; Jonathan Legate, Kwana of KwanaWrites; Janell of Isabella&Max; Kate of Centsational Girl; Amy of Masion Decor; Tanya of Save the Date for Cupcakes; Juliann of Create Girl; Stephanie of Sabbesspot; Lindsay of Everything LEB; Sarah of LiveLaughShop; Lindsay of A Design Story; Emily of Perfectly Put Together; Traci Zeller; Sarah of Thrifty Decor; Bryn Alexandra; Teresa of The Stamford Wife and many more! (This is just from the top of my head). I somehow missed a few other people I really wanted to chat with even though we were all in the same room. But can you believe I got to meet all of those talented bloggers in one night???I had such a great time!! The only downside was seeing this photo of myself that sent me into a shame circle all weekend long. I know its only a photo but wow, I look like a three chinned slow witted monster here. Ugh.

# Customizing opencode

opencode validates its own config strictly and refuses to start when a field
is wrong. The shapes below cover the common surface area, but they are a
**summary, not the source of truth**.

## Full schema reference

The authoritative list of every config option — with field types, enums,
defaults, and descriptions — lives in the published JSON Schema:

**<https://opencode.ai/config.json>**

If a field is not documented in this skill, or you need to confirm an exact
shape before writing config, **fetch that URL and read the schema directly**
rather than guessing. opencode hard-fails on invalid config, so the cost of a
wrong shape is a broken startup.

Independently, every `opencode.json` should declare
`"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json"` so the user's editor catches
mistakes as they type.

## Applying changes

Config is loaded once when opencode starts and is not hot-reloaded. After
saving changes to `opencode.json`, an agent file, a skill, a plugin, or any
other config-time file, **tell the user to quit and restart opencode** for
the changes to take effect. The running session will keep using the
already-loaded config until then.

## Where files live

| Scope                         | Path                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project config                | `./opencode.json`, `./opencode.jsonc`, or `.opencode/opencode.json` (opencode walks up from the cwd to the worktree root) |
| Global config                 | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (NOT `~/.opencode/`)                                                                   |
| Project agents                | `.opencode/agent/<name>.md` or `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`                                                               |
| Global agents                 | `~/.config/opencode/agent(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                   |
| Project commands              | `.opencode/command/<name>.md` or `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`                                                           |
| Global commands               | `~/.config/opencode/command(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                 |
| Project skills                | `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                                      |
| Global skills                 | `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                             |
| External skills (auto-loaded) | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                    |

Configs from each scope are deep-merged. Project overrides global. Unknown
top-level keys in `opencode.json` are rejected with `ConfigInvalidError`.

## opencode.json

Every field is optional.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "username": "string",
  "model": "provider/model-id",
  "small_model": "provider/model-id",
  "default_agent": "agent-name",
  "shell": "/bin/zsh",
  "logLevel": "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR",
  "share": "manual" | "auto" | "disabled",
  "autoupdate": true | false | "notify",
  "snapshot": true,
  "instructions": ["AGENTS.md", "docs/style.md"],

  "skills": {
    "paths": [".opencode/skills", "/abs/path/to/skills"],
    "urls": ["https://example.com/.well-known/skills/"]
  },

  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and documentation conventions"
    },
    "sdk": {
      "repository": "owner/sdk",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for SDK implementation details",
      "hidden": true
    }
  },

  "agent": {
    "my-agent": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "description": "...",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny" }
    }
  },

  "command": {
    "deploy": { "description": "...", "template": "..." }
  },

  "provider": {
    "anthropic": { "options": { "apiKey": "..." } }
  },
  "disabled_providers": ["openai"],
  "enabled_providers": ["anthropic"],

  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "environment": {}
    },

    "opencode-gemini-auth",
    "opencode-foo@1.2.3",

    ["opencode-bar", { "option": "value" }]
  ],

  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny",
    "bash": { "git *": "allow", "*": "ask" }
  },

  "formatter": false,
  "lsp": false,

  "experimental": {
    "primary_tools": ["edit"],

  },

  "tool_output": { "max_lines": 200, "max_bytes": 8192 },

  "compaction": { "auto": true, "tail_turns": 15 }
